title: How to Lose Time and Money

Choose conditions where the most urgent recurring problem is one the company wants solved, and keep unavoidable fundraising bounded to a deliberate short interval.
title: The Top Idea in Your Mind

title: The Acceleration of Addictiveness

title: The Future of Startup Funding

title: What We Look for in Founders

title: Founder Control

Evaluate an odd early idea through founder resourcefulness, direct observation of users, and the team's ability to let the product morph; treat in-person user hunting as stronger evidence than surface plausibility.

title: Subject: Airbnb

candidate_workflows: When legislation is too slow to address a harmful industry practice, coordinate a short public behavioral commitment that makes compliance and refusal visible even when the pledge is not legally binding.

title: The Patent Pledge

candidate_workflows: Compare founder locations by whether starting a startup feels normal and valued there and by the density of chance encounters with people who can supply specialized help.

title: Why Startup Hubs Work

candidate_workflows: Map acquisition to the discovery channels available in the current market, and redesign the website as a funnel toward an interactive trial rather than assuming present-day distribution methods always existed.
Audit cost to serve at the heaviest-user boundary before choosing flat pricing, and make infrastructure decisions from observed operational failure risk rather than fashion.

title: Snapshot: Viaweb, June 1998

candidate_workflows: Audit the idea list for opportunities unconsciously filtered out because they require user conversations, institutional deals, regulation, fraud control, or other unpleasant work; distinguish necessary work on a valuable path from seeking pain for its own sake.

When estimating feasibility, include the founders' ability to grow with progressively harder problems instead of assuming present capability is fixed.
title: Schlep Blindness

candidate_workflows: Test resourcefulness by giving a founder one useful lead or one compact piece of advice and observing whether they chase its implications to completion without being babysat.

Distinguish evidence-based rejection of advice from rationalizing a prior decision: resourceful teams examine even inconvenient implications with fresh eyes and can explain contrary user evidence or experiments.

title: A Word to the Resourceful

candidate_workflows: Notice fear and identity threat as filters that can hide ambitious startup ideas, then examine problems just on the feasible side of impossible without assuming every bad-looking idea is secretly good.

Approach a huge outcome through a deceptively small working wedge and an intense initial user group; describe the near-term product plainly so expectations and public opposition do not outrun evidence.

candidate_workflows: When technology changes distribution or enforceability, revisit what can sustainably be owned or charged for instead of assuming the old property and value-capture model remains viable.

title: Defining Property

Standardize a transaction that is currently haphazard, pairing clear terms with practical setup help and calm operational guidance rather than supplying money alone.

Batch several cases into a time-boxed program to learn faster, launch before the window closes, and preserve the structure only after observing that it works; choose the next location by participant density while adapting pragmatically to time constraints.
title: How Y Combinator Started

candidate_workflows: Choose writing when the objective is to develop and preserve good ideas; establish command of the subject, use plain words, and spend as long as needed improving each sentence.
Choose live speaking when engagement or motivation matters, and work from an outline when full attention to the audience is more important than sentence-level precision.
Allocate rehearsal versus rewriting according to the communication goal, and read drafts aloud at least once to expose awkward language before delivery.
title: Writing and Speaking

candidate_workflows: Identify high-cost mistakes caused by omission rather than active choice, invert each recurring omission into a short positive command, and pin the commands to the top of the task system used every day.

title: The Top of My Todo List

candidate_workflows: Evaluate a startup's chance of an extreme outcome separately from its chance of ordinary success, and calibrate portfolio breadth to the 1000x variation in returns rather than intuitive outcome ranges.

Treat safe-looking execution and easy fundraising as weak or potentially negative proxies when selecting outliers; examine whether an odd founder or bad-looking idea has a higher chance of succeeding enormously.

Do not optimize Demo Day fundraising rate merely because it is measurable; define the portfolio metric that actually drives returns, then check whether near-universal fundability signals excessive conservatism.
Keep the founder's desired ambition separate from the investor's portfolio economics: a broad portfolio can support founders who choose early sale, slower growth, or continued ownership.
title: Black Swan Farming

candidate_workflows: Decide whether an opportunity is a startup by testing both demand scale and the ability to reach and serve that market; do not infer startup status from age, technology, venture funding, or an exit plan.
Map the company to the startup S-curve: expect slow or no growth during discovery, use the rapid-growth ascent as the startup compass, and expect later slowdown as internal and market limits appear.

Follow sustained growth as evolutionary pressure even when it changes the original idea, but reject manufactured activity, uneconomic acquisition, and high-churn curves that corrupt the compass.

title: Startup = Growth

candidate_workflows: Build a hardware opportunity map across crowdfunding, connected controllers, component improvements, prototyping tools, manufacturing access, and online retail instead of evaluating hardware from an outdated category average.
Distinguish persistent investor aversion from changed operating economics; treat founder experiments and batch performance as leading indicators while investor consensus trails.

title: The Hardware Renaissance

candidate_workflows: Start with a problem the founders have, can build for, and understand better than others; ask who needs even a crude version enough to overcome its actual adoption effort, require stronger evidence where enterprise channels, switching, or integration raise that effort, prefer narrow and deep demand, and look for a path beyond the first niche.

Turn off schlep and unsexy filters, inspect ignored sophisticated users and newly feasible waves, and use willingness to do hard real-world work as an advantage rather than a reason to avoid the problem.

title: How to Get Startup Ideas

candidate_workflows: When startup costs fall, reassess inherited financing assumptions: start from the capital the company needs and the equity founders are willing to sell instead of an investor's target ownership percentage.

Treat founders as the customers of an investment product: collect recurring complaints, identify the unsatisfied demand behind them, and change the investment process to solve it.
When evaluating investor control, distinguish selection and support from micromanagement; judge the arrangement by whether founder control and aligned service improve company outcomes.
title: Startup Investing Trends
